title: Analog or Digital?
author: Stephen Fitzpatrick
source: Teaching in the Age of AI (fitzyhistory.substack.com), September 22, 2026
summary: History teacher Stephen Fitzpatrick reports that two weeks into the school year his classroom, like many others, has largely closed its laptops and returned to marble composition books, driven by the reckoning over screen time and fears about AI. He welcomes the change in part, recalling years of screens serving as barriers to engagement, and credits paper with more silent work time and better attention. He is equally frank about the costs: losing the real-time visibility and paper trail of a learning management system, the logistics of collecting handwritten work, students with device accommodations, and above all the erosion of instructional time for content-heavy courses. His central argument is that the return to paper looks more like a defensive retreat than a strategy, especially since his own advanced AI workflows convince him the tools offer students genuinely novel opportunities. He ends by urging schools to face AI with students rather than against them and to stop treating the issue as merely a cheating problem.
points: Fitzpatrick sees classrooms nationwide dialing back screens, with major assessments moving into class to address the authenticity problem.
Paper brings more silent time on task and fewer hidden distractions, which matters for teenagers whose prefrontal cortex is still developing.
The costs include lost LMS visibility, messy logistics, students needing devices for accommodations, and less time to teach content.
He argues most students would rather learn from a person than a chatbot, while also questioning why AI's real benefits are withheld from students.
Treating AI as a cheating problem nearly four years after ChatGPT is, in his view, a way of playing defense rather than a real answer.
quotes: For now, though I understand there are sound pedagogical reasons for it, the return to paper still strikes me more as a defensive retreat than an actual strategy.

It was not uncommon to walk past classroom after classroom with student screens serving as barriers to engagement, making it virtually impossible for teachers to verify on a moment-to-moment basis what students were doing.
When students face an empty page, brows furrowed, pencils poised, wearing the anguished look of someone searching for something to say, thinking is clearly happening.

But the most significant loss is more insidious: the quiet erosion of time. It hits hardest in courses built around a lot of content. Bringing more student work into the room means less time to introduce and explain new concepts.

They'll turn to one when they need to, but given the choice, most would much rather learn from a person. Teachers are the adults who set up the lessons, fill in the gaps, redirect the class in response to the situation, and read the room.
Resisting the technology may feel like the right thing to do in the current moment (and I'm doing my fair share of it this fall), but it seems mostly like playing defense.
Treating it as a cheating problem nearly four years after ChatGPT arrived, however, is not an answer. Neither is continuing to ignore it.
